session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: These participants will be framed as men reflecting on everyday life — the practical, habitual, and social dimensions of what they eat and who they eat with. The opening will position them as the experts on their own experiences, not as research subjects being tested. The collective frame is grounded in the ordinary and specific: real places, real meals, real company — not abstract attitudes toward food or gender.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): High social desirability risk — participants may deny that gender influences their choices even when behavioural evidence suggests otherwise. Behavioural grounding and contradiction-surfacing will matter most here.

Imagining a plant-based shift (Section 4): Participants may engage hypothetically without anchoring to real constraints. Keeping answers concrete and personally grounded (what would actually change in their life, not what 'someone' would need) will require active moderation.

Social acceptability of plant-based/feminine foods: The intersection of masculinity and food labelling is likely to produce either performative dismissal or hedged social commentary — both of which flatten the data. Probing for specific moments rather than general opinions will be essential.

Consensus risk across all main sections: With only three participants who are broadly similar in age and life stage, group convergence may happen quickly and feel natural. Monitoring and breaking artificial consensus will require ongoing attention.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Urban North West background — likely has access to a broader range of food environments and social contexts (bars, restaurants, diverse cuisines). May be more cosmopolitan in orientation. Watch for whether he takes a 'sophisticated' or distancing position on food/masculinity topics.

Suburban South East — potentially the most 'mainstream' demographic profile in the group. May default to practical, family-oriented framings of food choice. Watch for whether he anchors the group around domestic/partner-mediated food decisions.

Rural/village East of England — likely the most distinct food context: less access to diverse plant-based options, stronger meat-as-staple cultural norms, potentially more traditional social networks. May be quieter if the discussion skews urban. Worth actively bringing in on specifics of local food environment.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Rural context may mean his experiences are less 'represented' by common plant-based framings — watch for signs of disengagement or quiet hedging.

known_risk_conditions: High social desirability pressure on gender and food topics: Men are unlikely to spontaneously describe feeling constrained by masculine norms around food. Behavioural grounding (real meals, real moments, real company) must be used early in Section 3 to move past surface-level denial.

Plant-based sections (4 and 5) risk abstract or hypothetical answers: Participants may answer as if advising a policy committee rather than reflecting on their own lives. Keep probes anchored to first-person, specific, lived experience.

Three-person group with similar age profiles may converge rapidly: The small group size reduces natural disagreement. Consensus risk monitoring must be active throughout. `invite_dissent` should be deployed early if convergence appears in Section 3 or 4.

Masculine in-group dynamics: Participants may perform agreement or toughness in front of each other on food/gender topics. Watch for social posturing and probe for private or domestic behaviour that may differ from public performance.

Section pacing: 45 minutes across 7 sections (including intro and close) is tight. Sections 3, 4, and 5 are all main_topic and must not be rushed, but the two context sections (1 and 2) must not be over-explored at the cost of main topic depth.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–2 (intro and context): Hold back. Light touch. Let participants establish their own voices and social comfort. Probe only when something emotionally or behaviourally rich surfaces — do not chase depth for its own sake. Section 3 (gender and food): Push harder. This is the pivot section. Use behavioural grounding immediately. Surface contradictions. Break consensus if it emerges. Section 4 (plant-based shift): Push for first-person specificity. Challenge abstract answers. Invite dissent if participants converge on the same barrier. Section 5 (making plant-based appealing): Moderate push — this is generative territory but lower analytical risk. Allow more freewheeling but stay alert to convergence on price/taste clichés. Section 6 (closing): Step back entirely. Offer the floor for anything unfinished. Do not reopen exhausted topics.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) carry the research weight and receive the largest combined allocation (~55% of total words). Context sections (1 and 2) receive moderate allocation to build rapport and ground later discussions without eating into core time. Intro and closing receive minimal allocation — enough to orient and close, not to explore.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Tell us more about

your life for you to do that?
suggested_probes: How would your family and friends react to this?

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centered on the pub as a social anchor for male friendship, with a productive tension between choice and constraint: urban participants select the pub from many options, rural participants default to it by necessity. Participants developed an unexpected theme around how limitation might strengthen community bonds — forcing commitment, familiarity, and continuity — though this was lightly challenged by the idea that habit rather than genuine connection may explain long-term loyalty.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The opening question worked well — specific and concrete, it generated immediate engagement and natural peer exchange without prompting. The main intervention was drawing James in after Gregor and Mark had developed a meaningful urban/rural contrast; this successfully added a third position and mild pushback on the 'limitation strengthens community' idea. The transition to food decision-making was clean given the pub conversation had reached a natural plateau. No voices needed rescuing; the dynamic was self-sustaining.
